summary: A case study of the implementation of routing between the NSFNET and the DDN components, the MILNET and ARPANET. It is hoped to help extend interconnection to other administrative domains. No standards are specified.

plainLanguage.summary: Two big networks needed to share traffic. This tells the story of how they hooked up and agreed on directions.

questions: how did nsfnet and ddn connect
subtitle: Connecting two major research networks through controlled routing

tldr.problem: Two large federal research networks, NSFNET and DDN (Defense Data Network), needed to exchange traffic while maintaining separate administrative control.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a case study of two approaches: first through intermediate gateways running EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol), later through direct connections to Mailbridges—specialized route servers that both networks connect to directly.
tldr.outcome: The direct Mailbridge approach improved reliability and enabled load distribution, though architectural constraints of the DDN limited further performance optimization.

today: RFC 1133 is Informational and documents a case study of routing interconnection from 1989. The networks and technologies described have evolved significantly, but the document remains a historical record of early inter-domain routing engineering.

sections.title: Interconnecting Federal Research Networks
sections.content: The NSFNET backbone network connected multiple mid-level networks serving universities and research centers, and needed to exchange traffic with the DDN (Defense Data Network), which combined the MILNET and ARPANET. The RFC is a case study showing how routing between these administratively separate networks was implemented and evolved. Rather than specifying a standard, it documents practical lessons from the mid-1989 transition to a more effective interconnection architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Two separate networks run by different organizations needed to talk to each other. This document tells the story of how they connected and what they learned.

sections.title: The Early Approach: Gateways via the ARPANET
sections.content:
Until mid-1989, NSFNET and DDN were connected through intermediate routers that connected to the ARPANET, forming a chain between the two networks. These gateways ran the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) to exchange routing information with both NSFNET network switching systems (NSS) and DDN Mailbridges. Three gateways at different sites provided redundancy: starting at Cornell, University of Illinois, and Merit, later replaced at Pittsburgh Supercomputer Center and John von Neumann Supercomputer Center to maintain coverage after some connections closed.

Each gateway announced DDN networks to its co-located NSS with different metrics (cost values) so traffic would prefer the lowest-cost path, with other gateways serving as hot backups. In the reverse direction, NSS nodes announced NSFNET networks to the gateways, which redistributed them to the DDN via EGP, each using its local network's Autonomous System number.
sections.plainLanguage: The first method was like sending mail through relay stations. Each station knew where things should go and picked the best path based on how far away it was.

sections.title: Direct Mailbridge Connections
sections.content:
During the first half of 1989, DDN's Mailbridges—machines that switched traffic between the MILNET and ARPANET—added Ethernet adapters and directly connected to NSFNET backbone nodes. Two Mailbridges were installed: one at NASA-Ames in Moffett Field, California, and one at Mitre in Reston, Virginia. This direct connection eliminated the need to traverse the ARPANET and allowed the Defense Communication Agency and National Science Foundation to control the interconnection independently.

With two direct paths, the routing strategy split DDN networks between the two Mailbridges for load distribution. The Palo Alto NSS learned some networks with metric 10 and others with metric 12; the College Park NSS did the opposite, so each network was primarily routed through one Mailbridge with the other as backup. The split was initially random but discussions were underway to have DDN tell NSFNET which networks were geographically closer to which Mailbridge.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of relays, each network got direct phone lines to each other. Now traffic could be split to share the load, with one backup line for safety.

sections.title: Limitations and Optimization Challenges
sections.content:
Although the direct Mailbridge approach provided better redundancy and load sharing, it could not fully optimize traffic paths based on physical distance. For example, when an NSFNET network on the east coast sends traffic to a DDN network also on the east coast, the current setup might route it transcontinentally across both backbones, then back—crossing both networks unnecessarily. The ideal would be local exit points: east-coast networks meeting at the east Mailbridge, west-coast at the west bridge.

The DDN architecture presented fundamental constraints. It used a core routing model that did not expect the same network to be announced by multiple points, and its Mailbridges lacked physical topology information—they only knew IP-level routing, not which machines were physically nearby. Without this knowledge, they could not favor one exit point over another based on distance.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup worked well for reliability, but it still didn't always take the shortest path. Traffic might travel across the whole country and back when it could have taken a shorter route nearby.

sections.title: Administrative Control and Future Improvements
sections.content:
Each network administering body kept control over its own routing announcements. The NSFNET set metrics to announce each of its networks to both Mailbridges, preferring the one closer by hop count. Mid-level networks in NSFNET could request that their client networks be announced to the DDN, specifying whether it should be a primary or backup path.

The RFC notes that further improvements to achieve optimal traffic paths would likely require significant architectural changes within the DDN, particularly adding physical topology awareness and the ability to handle networks announced from multiple points. At publication, DDN and NSFNET were in discussions about adopting this approach to improve performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side decided what traffic got announced and at what cost. To do better would need both networks to understand physical distances, not just the logical routing.

left.title: Intermediate Gateways
left.desc: Traffic routed through intermediate gateways connected to both networks and the ARPANET, introducing additional hops.

right.title: Direct Mailbridges
right.desc: NSFNET nodes connect directly to DDN Mailbridges, reducing path length and enabling independent control at connection points.
